desc: Block device (disk) I/O by process top.
u: biotop - Block device (disk) I/O by process top.

This is top for disks.

This traces block device I/O (disk I/O), and prints a per-process summary every interval (by default, 1 second). The summary is sorted on the top disk consumers by throughput (Kbytes). The PID and process name shown are measured from when the I/O was first created, which usually identifies the responsible process.

For efficiency, this uses in-kernel eBPF maps to cache process details (PID and comm) by I/O request, as well as a starting timestamp for calculating I/O latency, and the final summary.

This works by tracing various kernel blk_*() functions using dynamic tracing, and will need updating to match any changes to these functions.

Since this uses BPF, only the root user can use this tool.

<dl><dt data-o="">-C</dt><dd>Don't clear the screen.</dd><dt data-o="">-r MAXROWS</dt><dd>Maximum number of rows to print. Default is 20.</dd><dt>interval</dt><dd>Interval between updates, seconds.</dd><dt>count</dt><dd>Number of interval summaries.</dd></dl>

Summarize block device I/O by process, 1 second screen refresh:
# biotop
Don't clear the screen:
# biotop -C
5 second summaries, 10 times only:
# biotop 5 10

<dl><dt>loadavg:</dt><dd>The contents of /proc/loadavg</dd><dt>PID</dt><dd>Cached process ID, if present. This usually (but isn't guaranteed) to identify the responsible process for the I/O.</dd><dt>COMM</dt><dd>Cached process name, if present. This usually (but isn't guaranteed) to identify the responsible process for the I/O.</dd><dt>D</dt><dd>Direction: R == read, W == write. This is a simplification.</dd><dt>MAJ</dt><dd>Major device number.</dd><dt>MIN</dt><dd>Minor device number.</dd><dt>DISK</dt><dd>Disk device name.</dd><dt>I/O</dt><dd>Number of I/O during the interval.</dd><dt>Kbytes</dt><dd>Total Kbytes for these I/O, during the interval.</dd><dt>AVGms</dt><dd>Average time for the I/O (latency) from the issue to the device, to its completion, in milliseconds.</dd></dl>

Since block device I/O usually has a relatively low frequency (< 10,000/s), the overhead for this tool is expected to be low or negligible. For high IOPS storage systems, test and quantify before use.

This is from bcc.

https://github.com/iovisor/bcc

Also look in the bcc distribution for a companion _examples.txt file containing example usage, output, and commentary for this tool.
